query: Taking nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 as the starting material, what single intervention could prevent its radiation-induced precipitation while retaining its negligible irradiation hardening and improving its suitability for practical bulk fabrication? Formulate one testable hypothesis for energetic-particle irradiation relevant to fusion service, including comparison with the unmodified alloy at approximately 8 dpa; identify the intervention and mechanism, predict quantitative or directional changes in precipitation, irradiation defects, and hardening, define the applicable irradiation and thermal boundaries, cite supporting prior evidence, and propose a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Substituting a minor fraction (~5 at.%) of Ta with Zr in nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 will suppress radiation‐induced Cr–V precipitation, while preserving the alloy’s inherently low irradiation hardening and enhancing its bulk sinterability via improved densification during powder metallurgy.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 with bimodal (nanocrystalline and ultrafine) grain size and a single-phase BCC structure that shows Cr–V precipitation under irradiation but negligible irradiation hardening.
generation.intervention: Introduce a ~5 at.% Zr substitution by replacing part of Ta (e.g. W38Ta31Zr5Cr15V11), leveraging Zr’s known effects on lattice distortion and grain boundary chemistry to modify short-range order and promote sintering.
generation.conditions: Energetic-particle irradiation to approximately 8 dpa at reactor-relevant temperatures (around 1073 K), combined with powder metallurgy processing (e.g. spark plasma sintering around 1600 °C) to assess bulk fabrication performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced lattice distortion and altered chemical short-range order from the Zr addition, along with preferential segregation of Zr at grain boundaries that both lowers the thermodynamic driving force for Cr–V clustering and stabilizes the nanostructure during sintering.
generation.mechanism: Zr’s larger atomic size and strong affinity for oxygen and solute elements can increase the mixing entropy and disrupt the local chemical ordering that drives Cr–V precipitation under irradiation. Simultaneously, Zr is known to promote densification in refractory alloys, thus making the material more amenable to bulk fabrication while maintaining abundant defect sinks.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified irradiation conditions, the Zr‐modified alloy should exhibit a significantly lower density and smaller size of Cr–V precipitates compared with the baseline. Nanoindentation should reveal similar or even slightly reduced irradiation‐induced hardening, and sintered bulk samples should show improved relative density and microstructural homogeneity.
generation.baseline: The undoped nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11, which under energetic-particle irradiation develops lamella‐like and quasi‐spherical Cr–V precipitates with a density of approximately 0.03 nm⁻² and shows only slight hardening.
generation.boundary: Tested under fusion-relevant energetic-particle irradiation conditions up to ~8 dpa at temperatures around 1073 K, and processed via powder metallurgy (e.g. spark plasma sintering at ~1600 °C) to evaluate bulk fabrication viability.
generation.uncertainty: While existing studies (e.g., PMC9572595 demonstrating excellent irradiation resistance in Zr-containing BCC alloys and PMC5434025 showing improved sintering in refractory HEAs) support the idea of using Zr to modify defect evolution and densification, it remains uncertain whether Zr will effectively suppress Cr–V precipitation in the W–Ta–Cr–V base system. This extrapolation combines findings from different alloy systems and processing routes; moreover, potential changes in defect sink behavior due to Zr segregation (as noted in conflicting Hf studies, PMC10154406::web::015 and PMC10154406::web::016) introduce further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk specimens via powder metallurgy: one set of the baseline nanocrystalline W38Ta36Cr15V11 and one set of the Zr-modified alloy (W38Ta31Zr5Cr15V11). Subject both sets to energetic-particle irradiation up to ~8 dpa at around 1073 K. Post-irradiation, perform systematic microstructural characterization (using TEM and atom probe tomography) to quantify Cr–V precipitate density and size, and assess mechanical properties via nanoindentation. Additionally, evaluate sintered density and grain structure to appraise bulk fabrication quality.
measurements: Precipitate density and size (nm and nm⁻²) from TEM/APT
Relative density and grain size distribution from SEM and XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Zr-modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in Cr–V precipitate density or exhibits increased irradiation hardening relative to the baseline, or if its bulk sinterability does not improve (e.g. reduced relative density or presence of undesirable secondary phases), then the hypothesis is falsified.

A powder metallurgical technique using elemental powder mixing has been exploited by developing and analyzing a novel high-entropy alloy (WxTaTiVCr, simplified as xWs) and its derivative alloys for the development of reduced-activation alloys for future fusion power plants. Various compositions realized by varying the W content from 32 to 90at.% with in-situ TiC were prepared by consolidating a powder mixture through spark plasma sintering at 1600 °C. The relative density of the alloys sintered at 1600 °C was found to increase with a decrease in the W content. The characterization of xWs samples by XRD showed the BCC crystal structure of the alloys. A microstructural examination by SEM-EDS revealed multiple phases in the microstructures as bright, gray and dark regions. Moreover, various W-rich phases were observed in the matrix of the sintered samples. An investigation of these phases under TEM and a selected-area diffraction pattern analysis disclosed the presence of TiC in the W-rich matrix, as observed in BSE images. AbstractMedium-entropy alloys (MEAs) are prospective structural materials for emerging advanced nuclear systems because of their outstanding mechanical properties and irradiation resistance. In this study, the microstructure and mechanical properties of three new single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) structured MEAs (Zr40Nb35Ti25, Zr50Nb35Ti15, and Zr60Nb35Ti5) before and after irradiation were investigated. It is shown that the yield strength and elongation after fracture at room temperature are greater than 900 MPa and 10%, respectively. Three MEAs were irradiated with 3 MeV Fe11+ ions to 8 × 1015 and 2.5 × 1016 ions/cm2 at temperatures of 300 and 500 °C, to investigate the irradiation-induced hardening and microstructure changes. Compared with most conventional alloys, the three MEAs showed only negligible irradiation hardening and even softening in some cases. After irradiation, they exhibit somewhat surprising lattice constant reduction, and the microstructure contains small dislocation loops. Neither cavities nor precipitates were observed.
